paragraphs: Neural scaling laws describe how prediction performance changes as training time, data, and model size increase. This paper studies these relationships through a random feature model trained with gradient descent. Because the model can be analyzed mathematically, it provides a way to connect observed scaling patterns to the dynamics of learning.

The analysis predicts why performance can improve with different power law exponents for training time and model size. This difference leads to an asymmetric prescription for allocating computation: increase training steps faster than the number of model parameters. The prediction is consistent with recent empirical observations, rather than establishing a universal allocation rule for every neural network.

The model also reproduces a change in how finite networks approach infinite-width behavior between early and late training. Finally, it explains how repeatedly using the same data can gradually widen the gap between training and test loss. Together, these results link resource allocation and generalization within one tractable account of training.
icml-2024-a-dynamical-model-of-neural-sc.tldr: A solvable training model explains several neural scaling patterns and predicts increasing training steps faster than model size when allocating compute.

paragraphs: When inputs are measurements collected over time, selecting useful variables means choosing among entire longitudinal features. This paper introduces FSFC, a method that jointly selects these features and predicts categorical outcomes. It targets high-dimensional settings in which the number of candidate features can substantially exceed the number of observed individuals or other statistical units.

FSFC combines logistic loss with functional inputs in a single optimization problem. To solve it, the authors use functional principal components and develop an adaptive version of the Dual Augmented Lagrangian algorithm. The approach treats variable selection and classification as connected tasks, with computational efficiency central to making their joint solution practical.

In simulations, FSFC achieves better classification accuracy and shorter computation times than the machine learning and deep learning methods considered. Its selected variables can also reduce dimensionality and improve other classifiers. A real-data application examines relationships involving four chronic diseases and health and demographic factors, demonstrating the method beyond simulated examples.
icml-2024-a-new-computationally-efficien.tldr: FSFC jointly selects longitudinal features and classifies outcomes, with reported gains in accuracy and computation time in high-dimensional settings.

paragraphs: Computing homotopy groups of spheres is a longstanding problem in algebraic topology. This paper explores how machine learning might help researchers understand the group-theoretic structure of their generators. Its immediate target is generating simplicial cycles in the setting of Wu’s formula, making the work a step toward that broader mathematical objective.

The central move is to translate cycle generation into a sequence-sampling problem. Valid outputs must belong to the intersection of algorithmically defined datasets related to Dyck languages. This reformulation connects the mathematical conditions governing cycles with a setting in which language models can be trained and evaluated on sequences.

The authors present language modelling approaches that use multiple labels associated with input sequences. They also provide the group-theoretic tools needed for the formulation and non-neural baselines for evaluation. The contribution is a concrete bridge between a topology problem and language modelling; the abstract reports evaluation of these approaches without claiming that they solve the general homotopy-group computation problem.
icml-2024-applying-language-models-to-al.tldr: The paper reformulates simplicial-cycle generation as constrained sequence sampling and evaluates language models that use multiple input labels.

paragraphs: Some expensive objectives are built from a network of functions, where intermediate outputs become inputs to later computations. Bayesian optimization can exploit this structure, but existing methods for general-purpose function networks evaluate the entire network at every iteration. That can spend resources unnecessarily when individual components are available for separate evaluation.

This paper introduces a knowledge gradient acquisition function that chooses both a node and the inputs at which to evaluate it. The choice accounts for evaluation cost, allowing each optimization step to query only part of the network. The authors also develop an efficient method for optimizing this acquisition function, addressing the computational work involved in deciding what to query.

Across several synthetic and real-world problems, the proposed approach outperforms existing function-network optimization methods and other benchmarks. Its practical significance lies in making partial evaluations part of the optimization strategy itself. The benefit applies to settings where components can actually be evaluated individually, rather than requiring every query to run the full computation.
icml-2024-bayesian-optimization-of-funct.tldr: A cost-aware Bayesian optimization method chooses individual function-network components to evaluate, improving results while reducing query costs.

paragraphs: Sampling from probability distributions that are difficult to work with directly is a central task for Monte Carlo methods, variational inference, and combinations of the two. Comparing these approaches is complicated when studies use different tasks and performance measures. A method’s apparent progress can be hard to interpret without a shared evaluation setting.

This paper introduces a benchmark with a standardized collection of tasks and a broad set of assessment criteria. The aim is to make comparisons more consistent and informative across sampling methods. Rather than reducing evaluation to one measure, the benchmark examines different aspects of performance that can reveal distinct strengths and weaknesses.

The authors give particular attention to mode collapse, where a sampler fails to represent parts of the target distribution. They study existing ways to measure this behavior and introduce additional metrics. The resulting evaluation offers evidence for understanding tradeoffs among methods and choosing approaches for particular tasks, while providing a common reference for assessing future developments.
icml-2024-beyond-elbos-a-large-scale-eva.tldr: A standardized sampling benchmark combines broad performance criteria with new mode-collapse metrics to clarify methods’ strengths and weaknesses.

paragraphs: Methods such as deep ensembles and Bayesian neural networks can improve uncertainty estimates, but their model size and prediction latency can make deployment expensive. Density-Softmax addresses this computational problem with a deterministic framework that does not require sampling at test time. The goal is useful uncertainty estimation and robustness with a smaller prediction-time burden.

The framework combines softmax with a density function built on a Lipschitz-constrained feature extractor. This construction makes predictions sensitive to distance in the learned feature space. The authors theoretically characterize the model as a solution to a minimax uncertainty-risk problem and show how its distance awareness reduces standard softmax’s overconfidence under distribution shifts.

Experiments report uncertainty and robustness results competitive with state-of-the-art techniques, alongside fewer model parameters and lower test-time latency. These findings support the framework’s relevance to resource-constrained devices and real-time applications. The stated result is competitive empirical performance with greater efficiency, rather than a claim that the method surpasses every alternative on every measure.
icml-2024-density-softmax-efficient-test.tldr: Density-Softmax combines feature-space density with softmax to deliver competitive uncertainty and robustness with lower test-time cost.

paragraphs: Adapting large pretrained models to sensitive data with differential privacy can require substantial computation or changes to the network architecture. This paper proposes DP-BiTFiT, which applies private fine-tuning to bias terms. By training only about 0.1% of the parameters, the method aims to retain strong task performance while sharply reducing the work required for adaptation.

DP-BiTFiT does not modify the network architecture and is presented as model agnostic. The authors report that it matches state-of-the-art accuracy among private algorithms while achieving the efficiency of standard BiTFiT. They describe the additional time and memory overhead associated with differential privacy as almost eliminated, rather than claiming that privacy has no computational cost.

Across the evaluated tasks, DP-BiTFiT is 2–30 times faster and uses 2–8 times less memory than private full fine-tuning. It is also faster than standard full fine-tuning. This efficiency enables private adaptation for long text sequences and high-resolution images, settings the abstract identifies as computationally difficult for existing methods.
icml-2024-differentially-private-bias-te.tldr: DP-BiTFiT privately fine-tunes only bias parameters, matching reported leading private accuracy while substantially reducing time and memory costs.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate an individual’s evolving event intensity from static characteristics and measurements recorded at irregular times. Intensity describes the rate at which events occur in a counting process. The task therefore involves learning how event rates change with a person’s or system’s observed history, rather than assigning one fixed rate.

The authors model intensity through a controlled differential equation and build a neural estimator using neural controlled differential equations. They then show that, under sufficient regularity conditions, this model can be expressed linearly in signature space. That result yields a second estimator, CoxSig, providing two estimation approaches connected by the same underlying formulation.

The paper supplies theoretical learning guarantees for both estimators and evaluates them on simulated and real-world data from finance, predictive maintenance, and food supply chain management. These applications demonstrate the approach across different event-prediction settings. The conditional linearization is especially useful conceptually: it links a differential-equation model of changing intensity to a signature-based estimator without asserting that this connection holds without regularity assumptions.
icml-2024-dynamic-survival-analysis-with.tldr: Controlled differential equations connect two theoretically supported estimators of individual event rates from static and irregular time-series data.

paragraphs: Maintaining a decision tree becomes difficult when examples can continually be inserted or deleted. This paper considers even adversarial update sequences and provides an algorithm with guarantees on both tree quality and the time needed for each update. The time guarantee concerns the slowest individual update, rather than only an average across many changes.

For Gini gain, the algorithm keeps each node’s split within beta of the optimum with update time O(d beta^-3 log^4 n), where d counts features and n is the maximum dataset size. This connects a local split-quality tolerance to maintenance cost. Similar guarantees cover variance and information gain, classification and regression, and boosted trees.

The results show how popular tree-building approaches, including ID3 and C4.5, can be made dynamic efficiently. A lower bound requires at least linear dependence on the feature count. Separately, under either of two stated complexity conjectures, update time must depend polynomially on inverse beta, showing a conditional computational cost for demanding increasingly accurate splits.
icml-2024-fully-dynamic-approximate-deci.tldr: A dynamic decision-tree algorithm guarantees approximate split quality and worst-case update times under adversarial insertions and deletions.

paragraphs: Genie learns to generate interactive virtual environments from unlabelled Internet videos. Users can prompt it with text or visual material, including synthetic images, photographs, and sketches, and then act within the generated world frame by frame. The central contribution is learning this controllability without ground-truth labels specifying which actions produced the training videos.

The 11-billion-parameter model combines three components: a spatiotemporal video tokenizer, an autoregressive dynamics model, and a latent action model. Together, these provide a representation of video, a model of how it unfolds, and a learned space of actions. The authors present the resulting system as a foundation world model capable of generating a wide variety of environments.

The learned action space also supports training agents to imitate behaviors shown in previously unseen videos. This extends the contribution beyond producing interactive scenes to using video as a source of behavioral learning. The abstract frames generalist agents as a future possibility opened by this capability, rather than an outcome already established by Genie.
icml-2024-genie-generative-interactive-e.tldr: Genie learns action-controllable virtual worlds from unlabelled videos and provides latent actions that support imitation from unseen videos.

paragraphs: HAMLET is a graph transformer framework for solving partial differential equations with neural networks. Its design directly incorporates information about the differential equation into the solution process. The paper targets a framework usable across different physical simulation settings, with particular attention to accommodating varied geometries and ways of presenting inputs.

The key architectural choice is a set of modular input encoders used with graph transformers. This modularity gives greater control over parameter correspondence and makes the framework adaptable to arbitrary geometries and different input formats. The approach therefore connects how a problem is represented at the input with how the neural model uses its equation-specific information.

The authors report robustness as data complexity and noise increase, along with improved resilience and performance when training data are limited. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HAMLET can outperform current PDE techniques. These findings support its usefulness across multiple domains and difficult data conditions, while the abstract’s performance claim remains one of demonstrated capability rather than guaranteed superiority for every equation.
icml-2024-hamlet-graph-transformer-neura.tldr: HAMLET uses modular equation-aware encoders and graph transformers to solve PDEs across varied geometries, with reported robustness and performance gains.

paragraphs: This paper examines how models memorize patterns that are uncorrelated with the task they are supposed to learn. It seeks a precise theoretical account of this behavior, complementing empirical studies of memorization. The analysis separates memorization into two contributions, making it possible to distinguish different reasons a spurious pattern can influence a model.

The first contribution is stability: how sensitive the model is to an individual training example. The second is feature alignment between the spurious pattern and the full sample. The authors characterize this alignment for random feature regression and neural tangent kernel regression, revealing how the model and its activation function affect memorization.

Within the analyzed setting, the authors prove that spurious-feature memorization weakens as generalization capability improves. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 show that the theory has predictive power on standard datasets. The result connects memorization to both sensitivity to training examples and the representation of patterns, rather than treating it as a phenomenon explained by stability alone.
icml-2024-how-spurious-features-are-memo.tldr: The paper characterizes spurious-feature memorization through model stability and feature alignment in random feature and neural tangent kernel regression.

paragraphs: Neural additive models make predictions by combining separate neural subnetworks for individual input features. This structure helps expose how each feature contributes to a prediction. However, the structure alone does not supply calibrated uncertainty or mechanisms for choosing relevant features and interactions. This paper develops a Bayesian treatment to address those gaps.

The proposed Laplace-approximated neural additive models provide credible intervals for individual subnetworks, adding uncertainty information to their feature-wise contributions. They also estimate marginal likelihood and use an empirical Bayes procedure for implicit feature selection. These additions connect interpretability with assessments of uncertainty and relevance within the same modelling framework.

A third component ranks pairs of features as candidates for second-order interactions in subsequently fine-tuned models. Pair ranking offers a way to decide which interactions deserve consideration while retaining the additive model as a starting point. The authors report improved empirical performance on tabular datasets and challenging medical tasks, supporting the practical value of these Bayesian additions in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-improving-neural-additive-mode.tldr: Bayesian extensions give neural additive models credible intervals, implicit feature selection, and interaction rankings, with improved empirical performance.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a nonlinear dynamical system from observations becomes more complicated when measurements come in different forms. A scientific dataset might combine continuous recordings, counts, and categorical labels. This paper develops a framework that brings such observations together to learn a shared account of the underlying dynamics, addressing multimodal integration within dynamical systems reconstruction.

The method uses a multimodal variational autoencoder to produce a sparse teaching signal for a reconstruction model. That signal guides training through recent dynamical reconstruction techniques. Different kinds of observations are connected within one latent dynamical space, allowing information from several measurement sources to contribute to the reconstructed system.

The framework can also reconstruct dynamics from symbolic class labels alone. After training, it is fully generative: the authors report trajectories with the same geometric and temporal structure as the ground-truth system. This makes the contribution more than an alignment of different observation types; the learned representation supports generating evolving behavior with the structure of the system being studied.
icml-2024-integrating-multimodal-data-fo.tldr: A multimodal autoencoder guides dynamical reconstruction, enabling joint generative modelling from mixed measurements or even class labels alone.

paragraphs: Message-passing graph neural networks are often compared with the Weisfeiler–Leman test by asking which graphs they can distinguish. Earlier equivalence constructions required feature dimensions that increased with graph size. This paper addresses the gap between those theoretical constructions and practical architectures, whose feature vectors usually have a fixed dimension.

The authors show that one-dimensional feature vectors suffice for equivalence to the test when the activation is any non-polynomial analytic function, such as sigmoid. The dimension can remain one regardless of graph size. The activation condition is part of the result: the paper establishes this sufficiency for the stated class of functions.

The proof relies on preserving linear independence over rational numbers rather than over real numbers when representing multisets. Combining this weaker independence requirement with properties of analytic functions lets the construction simulate successive test iterations without increasing feature dimension. The result changes what dimension is theoretically needed for distinguishing power, establishing that graph-size-dependent vectors are unnecessary under these activation assumptions.
icml-2024-on-dimensionality-of-feature-v.tldr: With any non-polynomial analytic activation, one-dimensional MPNN features suffice to match the Weisfeiler–Leman test’s distinguishing power.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that machine learning can help evaluate whether regulation reduces online harms. It focuses on the European Union’s Digital Services Act as a policy response to harmful platform practices, including the spread of disinformation. The central question is how to assess the regulation’s downstream impact when the relevant practices are opaque.

The authors analyze possible limitations in the Act’s provisions and identify methodological obstacles to measuring its effects. These include obtaining appropriate data, separating the marginal effect of regulation from other influences, and transferring conclusions across contexts. Addressing these obstacles is necessary for the research agenda they advocate, rather than an outcome the abstract claims has already been achieved.

The paper’s position is that machine learning’s harmful uses should not obscure its potential role in regulatory assessment. It calls for research that turns data-driven methods into evidence about policy impacts on online harms. Its contribution is an argument and methodological agenda for evaluation, rather than a reported numerical estimate of the Act’s effectiveness.
icml-2024-position-machine-learning-powe.tldr: This position paper advocates machine learning research to assess the Digital Services Act’s effects while addressing data access, attribution, and generalization barriers.

paragraphs: This paper sharpens the analysis of standard differentially private gradient descent for linear regression with squared error loss. Under modest assumptions on the input, the authors characterize the distribution of the model iterate at every training step. This distributional view supports conclusions about both prediction accuracy and uncertainty caused by the algorithm.

With a suitable fixed choice of hyperparameters, the required sample count depends only linearly on data dimension. This matches the dimensional dependence of ordinary least squares and recent private methods using sophisticated adaptive gradient clipping. The comparison concerns dependence on dimension, so it does not assert that all aspects of private and non-private estimation have identical costs.

The same analysis yields confidence intervals for the empirical optimizer, meaning the optimizer associated with the observed dataset. These intervals automatically adapt to the algorithm’s variance on that particular dataset. Synthetic-data experiments validate the theoretical results, connecting a tighter account of the training process to both improved accuracy bounds and dataset-specific uncertainty estimation.
icml-2024-private-gradient-descent-for-l.tldr: A distributional analysis of private gradient descent yields linear dimension dependence in sample complexity and dataset-adaptive confidence intervals.

paragraphs: Neural active learning chooses which examples to label so that a model can learn from a small labelled subset. Two common strategies prioritize uncertain examples or diverse examples. This paper offers a shared explanation for their success by studying which features the neural network has learned and which remain missing from its representation.

The analysis uses a feature-noise data model containing features that differ in learning difficulty, together with two-layer neural networks selecting examples from a pool. Within this setting, both query strategies tend to prioritize samples containing features that have not yet been learned. This gives a common feature-learning interpretation to selection criteria that initially look different.

The authors prove that this shared behavior enables small test error with a small labelled set. Passive selection, by comparison, inadequately learns the remaining features in the analyzed setting and needs substantially more labels to reduce error sufficiently. Experiments support these findings. The theoretical explanation is grounded in the specified data and network model, rather than claiming that either strategy succeeds under all conditions.
icml-2024-provably-neural-active-learnin.tldr: Under a feature-noise model, uncertainty and diversity sampling both succeed by selecting examples containing features the network has yet to learn.

paragraphs: Covariance matrices appear in many machine learning tasks, and combining them calls for an appropriate notion of an average. This paper studies the Fréchet mean on the space of symmetric positive definite matrices, also known as the Karcher or geometric mean. The object being estimated is therefore a mean defined through the geometry of this matrix space.

The authors introduce an estimator based on random matrix theory and advanced statistical tools. They identify a particularly useful setting: there is limited sample support, but many matrices need to be averaged. The method addresses estimation of the geometric mean in this regime, where the quantity of matrices and the sample support behind them are separate considerations.

Evaluation uses synthetic data as well as real EEG and hyperspectral datasets. The authors report substantially better performance than state-of-the-art methods in these experiments. The contribution is an improved statistical approach to a matrix-averaging operation used across machine learning, with empirical evidence from both controlled data and two different real-world data types.
icml-2024-random-matrix-theory-improved-.tldr: A random matrix theory estimator improves geometric averaging of covariance matrices, especially with low sample support and many matrices.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether unsupervised representation learning remains identifiable when the data only approximately satisfy a model’s assumptions. Identifiability concerns whether the hidden structure can be determined from observations, allowing specified ambiguities. The authors formalize robustness to slight misspecification through two related analyses of nonlinear mixing functions.

First, they consider mixing that is close, in a suitable distance, to a local isometry. Using existing rigidity results, they show that this mixing can be identified up to linear transformations and small errors. Second, they analyze independent component analysis when observations are an invertible linear mixture plus a small nonlinear perturbation, showing approximate recovery of both the mixing matrix and independent components.

Together, these results establish approximate identifiability for nonlinear independent component analysis with almost-isometric mixing. The significance is that exact membership in a restrictive model class can be relaxed in the studied settings. The guarantees retain specific closeness and perturbation assumptions, providing a step toward understanding real-world misspecification rather than unrestricted nonlinear recovery.
icml-2024-robustness-of-nonlinear-repres.tldr: The paper proves approximate identifiability for nonlinear ICA under almost-isometric mixing and analyzes recovery under small nonlinear perturbations.

paragraphs: Understanding a multivariate system requires examining relationships that involve several variables together. Pairwise analyses can miss this structure. This paper focuses on O-information, a quantity that summarizes the balance between information redundancy and synergy, helping characterize how information is shared or emerges collectively across a system’s variables.

Although O-information offers a scalable description of higher-order dependence, its practical computation has been restricted to simplified cases. The authors introduce SΩI, a score-based estimation method that uses a single model. They present it as enabling O-information computation without the restrictive assumptions about the system that have limited its practical use.

Experiments validate the method on synthetic data and demonstrate its effectiveness in a real-world use case. The contribution is therefore an estimation approach that makes an existing information-theoretic quantity more usable for complex data. Its significance lies in broadening access to the synergy–redundancy balance, so that analysis can address collective relationships rather than relying only on comparisons between pairs of variables.
icml-2024-s-i-score-based-o-information-.tldr: SΩI uses a single score-based model to estimate the synergy–redundancy balance in multivariate systems without restrictive system assumptions.

paragraphs: AI debate aims to make difficult judgments manageable by having competing systems expose the parts of a claim that need checking. This paper addresses a computational obstacle in an earlier debate framework: the honest strategy was assumed able to simulate deterministic AI systems for an exponential number of steps. That assumption limited the framework’s applicability.

The authors design new debate protocols in which the honest strategy can succeed using only polynomially many simulation steps. The protocols also handle stochastic AI systems, extending the setting beyond deterministic behavior. These changes jointly address how much computation honest participation requires and what kinds of systems the debate can verify.

The guarantee still holds when the dishonest strategy is allowed exponentially many simulation steps. Within the proposed protocols, this establishes a strong asymmetry: successful honest behavior does not require matching the opponent’s simulation budget. The contribution is a theoretical route toward more scalable debate-based alignment verification, with its success guarantee attached to the designed protocols and their formal setting.
icml-2024-scalable-ai-safety-via-doubly-.tldr: New debate protocols let an honest strategy verify stochastic AI systems with polynomial simulation effort despite an exponentially resourced dishonest opponent.

paragraphs: Noisy gradient descent is widely used for private learning, yet tightly quantifying its privacy leakage remains difficult. This paper improves analysis of privacy amplification by iteration using f-differential privacy. That framework captures the privacy-loss tradeoff directly and yields tighter accounting in other formulations, including epsilon-delta differential privacy and Rényi differential privacy.

The technical contribution is a construction of shifted interpolated processes. These processes unpack an existing shifted-divergences argument and allow the reasoning to extend beyond divergence-based relaxations of privacy. The authors obtain what they identify as the first exact privacy analysis in the foundational strongly convex optimization setting.

The techniques cover convex and strongly convex objectives, constrained and unconstrained optimization, and full, cyclic, and stochastic batches, including their combinations. They also recover an earlier f-differential privacy characterization of the exponential mechanism for strongly convex optimization and extend it to broader settings. The exactness claim concerns the stated strongly convex setting, while the wider contribution is a flexible analytical framework for several forms of private optimization.
icml-2024-shifted-interpolation-for-diff.tldr: Shifted interpolated processes tighten privacy accounting for noisy optimization and enable an exact analysis in a foundational strongly convex setting.

paragraphs: Combinatorial optimization involves discrete choices, which makes direct use of differentiable learning difficult. One approach replaces those choices with probabilistic objectives and then converts the result into a discrete solution. This paper addresses challenges in both stages, especially when problems include complex conditions such as those highlighted in its title.

The authors first specify theoretically justified targets for constructing probabilistic objectives and for derandomization, the process of obtaining a discrete output. They then derive objectives and conversion procedures for conditions that recur across different combinatorial problems. Treating both stages together addresses the gap between optimizing a probabilistic representation and producing a useful discrete solution.

The derivations are applied to several combinatorial optimization problems and evaluated on synthetic and real-world graphs. The authors report evidence validating the derivations and empirical advantages in both solution quality and speed. The contribution is a set of principled tools for handling recurring constraints, supported by experiments showing that improvements to objective construction and derandomization can work together.
icml-2024-tackling-prevalent-conditions-.tldr: The paper derives probabilistic objectives and derandomization procedures for common combinatorial constraints, reporting gains in solution quality and speed.

paragraphs: A sentence’s meaning can depend heavily on one word, even when the surrounding context is long. This paper studies whether a representation can remain sensitive to such a change. It calls this property word sensitivity and analyzes attention layers in a random-feature setting to understand one reason attention suits language tasks.

The authors show that random attention features have high word sensitivity: there exists an embedding-space vector that produces a large change in the feature map. Their argument depends critically on softmax. In comparison, standard random features have sensitivity proportional to the inverse square root of sentence length, so their response weakens as context grows.

The analysis connects sensitivity to generalization bounds. In the studied setting, standard random features cannot learn the required distinction between sentences differing in one word, whereas random attention features have greater generalization capability. Experiments using BERT-Base embeddings of IMDb reviews support the theory. The result establishes the existence of influential perturbations, rather than saying every single-word change strongly affects attention.
icml-2024-towards-understanding-the-word.tldr: In a random-feature analysis, softmax attention preserves sensitivity to influential word changes and supports stronger generalization than standard random features.
